At the Meryton assembly, when Bingley urged him to dance and pointed out Elizabeth sitting behind him, Mr. Darcy looked at her briefly, then coldly said, "She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt *me*; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men." He added that Bingley was wasting his time and should return to his partner. Elizabeth overheard this because Darcy was standing near enough for her to hear his conversation with Bingley. Rather than being crushed, "Elizabeth remained with no very cordial feelings towards him," but she turned the slight into a joke. She "told the story, however, with great spirit among her friends; for she had a lively, playful disposition, which delighted in anything ridiculous." Her resentment hardens later in Chapter V, where she assures her mother, "I believe, ma'am, I may safely promise you *never* to dance with him." This moment of wounded pride is what seeds her prejudice against Darcy for much of the novel.
